text: What did this workload cost us last month? In a hybrid, multi-cloud estate, that's really three separate questions wearing one trench coat. Azure, AWS, and your own data center each answer cost in a completely different format, and before you can build one unified view, you have to understand exactly why those three answers don't line up on their own.

Azure Cost Management prices usage by meter, with Reservations or Savings Plans discounts applied on top. AWS Cost Explorer and the underlying Cost and Usage Report price usage by line item, with their own separate Reserved Instance and Savings Plan model layered in. On-prem hardware doesn't answer the question at all in billing terms — there's no monthly invoice for a server you already own.

The real trap on the cloud side is committed-use discounts. Look at a one-year reserved instance paid up front: the raw number spikes in the purchase month and then shows as free every month after, which makes it look wildly cheap or wildly expensive depending on when you check. Amortized cost spreads that same commitment evenly across its term instead, and that's the figure a cross-cloud comparison actually needs — both Azure and AWS expose it for exactly this reason.

On-prem gets a different treatment: a fully-loaded estimate combining straight-line depreciation of the hardware with its ongoing power, cooling, support, and staff-time costs — comparable to a cloud opex figure, but always labeled as an estimate, never presented as exact invoice data. None of this rolls up without a shared join key, which is the same cost-center, environment, owner, and workload tags your FinOps work already established. The FinOps Foundation's FOCUS specification gives the industry a vendor-neutral schema to normalize billing data toward, rather than inventing your own column mapping from scratch.

Get the normalization right and you finally have one honest view of what a workload costs, wherever it runs. Next lesson turns to governance: instead of writing three different policy languages for Azure, AWS, and on-prem, you'll see how to define one set of controls and enforce them consistently everywhere, building on the governance model from an earlier course.
